summary: This chapter tells the story of Ravi, his mother Vidya, and his elderly Grandpa. Grandpa recently moved to the city to live with them and feels trapped by Vidya's overprotective nature. In an attempt to assert his independence, Grandpa craftily leaves the house alone. Ravi, trying to protect him, secretly follows but experiences a series of comical misadventures—getting scolded in a park, harassed by vendors, and thrown out of a ladies' salon—only to lose track of Grandpa entirely when he chases a stranger wearing Grandpa's cap. Returning home frantic, Ravi is relieved to find Grandpa safely asleep. Later, Grandpa surprises everyone with gifts. Vidya assumes he forgot Ravi's birthday was months ago, but Grandpa reveals it is actually *his* birthday, a tradition he always upholds. He playfully suggests Vidya needs 'Vitamin-M' for forgetting, and gives Ravi a detective book, subtly revealing he knew Ravi was tailing him all along. The story concludes by showing that despite his age, Grandpa's mind remains sharp and mischievous, subverting his family's assumptions about his frailty.

sa.q: Why did Ravi's mother wish someone would invent 'Vitamin-M'?
sa.a: Ravi's mother wished someone would invent a memory-improving vitamin called 'Vitamin-M' because Grandpa was becoming increasingly absent-minded, taking a double dose of medicine and getting lost on a walk, which caused her a lot of anxiety.

sa.q: Why did Grandpa have to come and live with Ravi's family in the city?
sa.a: Grandpa had to move in with Ravi's family because he had slipped and fallen in the garden of his own house late one evening and was unable to get up, spending the whole night outside. He was considered too old to live safely on his own.

sa.q: How did Grandpa feel about living in the city?
sa.a: Grandpa hated the noise and bustle of city life. He found the flat to be "poky" (small and cramped) and frequently spoke with longing about his quiet, old brick house with the large mango tree.

sa.q: What perplexes Ravi about Grandpa's memory?
sa.a: Ravi finds it perplexing that Grandpa can remember the exact details of thousands of historic chess games, such as moves by Karpov and Bobby Fischer, yet often forgets the names of people he meets frequently or forgets his way back home.

sa.q: What did Grandpa take with him when he went out?
sa.a: He took his shiny-black mahogany walking stick with a brass handle carved in the shape of an eagle's head, and put on his bright-yellow cap.

sa.q: Why was Ravi in a dilemma when Grandpa left the flat?
sa.a: Ravi knew Grandpa would feel hurt if he insisted on accompanying him, but he also knew his mother would be furious if she found out Ravi had let him go out on his own.

sa.q: What forbidden foods did Grandpa consume at the tea stall?
sa.a: Grandpa drank a sugary cup of tea and ate two bananas, both of which were banned items for him at home, and then tucked into an ice cream.

sa.q: Why was Ravi evicted from the shop next to the barber shop?
sa.a: Ravi mistakenly ducked into a Ladies' Hairdressing Salon while trying to secretly keep a closer eye on Grandpa, causing a volley of feminine shrieks, and was immediately thrown out.

sa.q: What surprise awaited Ravi when he confronted the man in the yellow cap on the bus?
sa.a: Ravi discovered that the man in the yellow cap was a total stranger. The stranger explained that a kind old gentleman in the barber shop (Grandpa) had insisted he take the cap because it was a hot day.

sa.q: What was the first thing Ravi heard when he got back home, frantic about Grandpa?
sa.a: He heard the gentle whirr of Grandpa snoring in his bedroom, which brought him great delight and relief.

sa.q: How did Grandpa explain his morning to Ravi's mother?
sa.a: Grandpa coolly said he had a quiet morning but claimed Ravi had just disappeared instead of staying at home to look after him, leaving Ravi confused and embarrassed.

sa.q: What was the real occasion for the gifts?
sa.a: It was actually Grandpa's birthday. It was his habit to give a gift to every child in the house on his birthday, a fact his daughter had forgotten despite marking it on the calendar.

sa.q: Why did Grandpa say his daughter needed 'Vitamin-M'?
sa.a: Grandpa jokingly said she needed 'Vitamin-M' for her memory because she had forgotten his birthday, turning her earlier comment about him needing it around on her.

sa.q: What gift did Grandpa give to Ravi and what did he say about it?
sa.a: He gave Ravi a thick hardcover book called 'The Best Detective Stories'. He solemnly suggested Ravi could pick up good tips on how to be a detective and avoid getting fooled when trailing a suspect, hinting he knew Ravi had followed him.

sa.q: (The Lost Child) What attracted the little boy as he lagged behind his parents on the way to the fair?
sa.a: The little boy was attracted by the toys in the shops, the dragon-flies and insects along the footpath, and the flowers in the grove.

sa.q: (The Lost Child) How did the boy's parents react when he pleaded for a toy?
sa.a: His father looked at him red-eyed in his familiar tyrant's way, giving a cold stare of refusal. His mother was tender and distracted him by pointing to a beautiful flowering mustard-field.

essay.q: Analyze the conflict between Grandpa and his daughter, Vidya. What does it reveal about their perspectives on his aging?
essay.a: The conflict between Grandpa and Vidya stems from the delicate balance between safety and independence in old age. Vidya, acting out of love and anxiety, is highly protective. After Grandpa's recent incidents of forgetfulness and his fall, she treats him with extreme caution, insisting he not go out alone and speaking to him in a loud, patronizing tone. To her, he is a frail figure needing constant supervision. Grandpa, however, deeply resents this loss of autonomy. Having been an independent lawyer who managed his own house for ten years after his wife's death, he feels treated like a 'prisoner' or a 'baby' in her cramped city flat. He perceives her over-protectiveness as a violation of his dignity. This conflict reveals the common struggle where well-meaning caretakers prioritize physical safety, while the elderly yearn for respect and the preservation of their former independence.

essay.q: Describe Ravi's comical experience of secretly following his Grandpa.
essay.a: Ravi's attempt to secretly tail Grandpa turns into a series of highly embarrassing misadventures. First, he hides behind an elephant-shaped bush in a children's park and is humiliated when a little boy's mother fiercely scolds him, forcing him to crawl away on all fours. Next, he hides behind a banyan tree near a tea stall, where local street vendors angrily surround him, mistakenly thinking he is a new vendor trying to take their spot. Finally, while trying to keep a closer eye on Grandpa near a barber shop, Ravi hurriedly ducks into the nearest shop, which turns out to be a Ladies' Hairdressing Salon. He is swiftly evicted amidst a volley of feminine shrieks. His well-intentioned efforts to be a stealthy detective result in a very funny sequence of clumsy mishaps, ending with the realization that he was chasing a complete stranger who was given Grandpa's cap.

essay.q: How does the ending of the story subvert the initial expectations about Grandpa's memory and capability?
essay.a: At the beginning of the story, Grandpa is portrayed as frail and absent-minded, with Vidya suggesting he needs a memory vitamin and forbidding him from going out alone. However, the ending completely flips this perception. Grandpa manages to outsmart Ravi, enjoying a day out on his own terms and safely returning home undetected. Furthermore, he remembers his own birthday and his tradition of giving gifts, while Vidya—who constantly worried about his memory—is the one who forgot. By giving Ravi a detective book and hinting at his trailing, Grandpa shows he was acutely aware of everything going on. He proves that despite physical frailty, his mind remains sharp and cunning, playfully turning the tables on his overprotective family.

essay.q: (The Lost Child) Discuss the contrast in the child's behaviour and desires before and after he loses his parents.
essay.a: Before the child loses his parents, he is full of life, joy, and desire. He is captivated by everything he sees at the fair—the toys, the dragon-flies, the gulab-jamuns, the garlands, the balloons, and the snake-charmer's music. He constantly asks his parents for these things, although he knows they will refuse. However, the moment he realizes his parents are missing, his entire world collapses. He is seized by sheer panic and fear. When a kind stranger rescues him and offers him all the things he had desperately wanted just moments before—a ride on the roundabout, listening to the snake-charmer, balloons, flowers, and sweets—the child rejects them all. His only cry becomes, "I want my mother, I want my father!" This stark contrast highlights that the child's sense of security and his love for his parents far outweigh any materialistic desires. Without his parents, the wonders of the fair lose all their charm and meaning.
